references.text: Parallel text in Deuteronomy that repeats the commandment against making a carved image or any likeness of what is in heaven, on earth, or in the water.
Prohibition against making idols, carved images, or cast images, which expands on the prohibition in the second commandment.
Moses warns the people against making carved images in the form of man, woman, animal, bird, creeping thing, or fish—an expansion of the image ban.
Warning against forgetting the covenant and making carved images, with a reminder that the Lord is a consuming fire, a jealous God.
Curse pronounced on anyone who makes a carved or cast image, an abomination to the Lord.
The prophet Isaiah asks whom God can be compared to and mocks those who make idols of metal and wood.
Isaiah's satire on idolatry and the futility of making gods out of wood and metal.
Paul speaks at the Areopagus and says we should not think that the divine being is like gold, silver, or stone, shaped by human art and imagination.
Paul describes how people exchanged the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man, birds, four-footed animals, and creeping things.
Clarifies the prohibition by specifying that it also applies to images in human form, expanding on the concept of 'likeness'.
Repetition of the prohibition in a new covenant situation, specifying that cast idols are also forbidden.
Expands the understanding of the prohibition by linking it to exclusivity: one must not make gods (of precious metal) alongside the Lord.
Direct parallel forbidding both turning to idols and making cast images, linked to God's identity.
